Help me understand this, Sofi doesn’t have to forego interest payments originate their loans. They can choose to keep it and collect future interest partners instead of selling it to investors when the loan worth less no?

Yes that's right they continue to collect interest and monthly payments. It's the risk of holding those loans, that is, defaulting or non payment by customers. However, their hedge or insurance is so far covering it. What they have lost is only the opportunity cost of getting it off the books quickly and then use the cash once again to originate new loans. When the originate new loans again and recycle the cash, it makes even more profit more quickly. The problem is loans locked in at lower rates are no longer as desired by buyers of loans. So Sofi are stuck with it. But they certainly still earn interest there, but the margin is thinning, because or rising rates they need to pay depositors with a rising rate macro environment

"Respect the academic breakdown, Professor, but your model leaves out the dynamic structural reality of SoFi’s balance sheet. You are evaluating their $27.5B 'Held for Sale' loan pool as if it carries pure macro duration risk without offsets.
First, SoFi’s macro hedging desk utilizes comprehensive interest rate derivative contracts explicitly designed to gain dollar-for-dollar value when benchmark yields expand, completely neutralizing the asset sensitivity compression you modelled.
Second, the assumption that loan demand has frozen is completely disproven by their latest audited metrics. SoFi didn't just hold loans; they grew originations by an explosive 69% year-over-year to a record $14.8B, while instantly offloading billions via high-margin fee deals to mega-funds like Basepoint Capital ($3B) and Sixth Street ($1B) [Context].
Finally, their Net Interest Margin expanded to an elite 5.98% precisely because their $45.5B sticky consumer deposit base gives them a fortress-like low cost of funding that legacy regionals cannot replicate.
The accounting marks are temporary noise. When a model deliberately isolates worst-case interest risks while completely ignoring multi-billion dollar institutional contract wins and expanding NIM margins, it starts sounding less like an objective academic analysis and more like a sophisticated short-bashing campaign in disguise. The raw GAAP profitability and capital leverage prove this is an absolute growth bargain. Looking forward to Anthony Noto clearing the tape on Tuesday morning! 📈🚀 #SOFI

I see another step toward a $100B+ deposit platform that could eventually support billions in annual revenue and completely change how the market values SoFi.

Everyone is talking about SOFIE. I think they're missing the point. The investment case for SoFi has never been about a single product, a single quarter, or a single earnings report. The real question is much bigger: What if Wall Street is still valuing SoFi as a bank while Anthony Noto is building something entirely different? Banks sell products. Platforms build ecosystems. Over the last few years, SoFi has expanded far beyond lending. It has built an increasingly connected ecosystem of banking, investing, credit, payments, and digital assets. Every new product makes the platform more valuable. Every new member creates more cross-selling opportunities. Every additional service strengthens customer retention.That is why SOFIE matters.Not because of the 4.4% yield. Not because it will immediately transform revenue.But because it is another signal pointing in the same direction: SoFi continues to expand the surface area of its ecosystem while most investors remain focused on the next quarter. The market loves to put companies into simple boxes. Today, many investors still put SoFi in the "bank" box. But if SoFi succeeds, that box may prove far too small.Because banks compete for deposits.Platforms compete to become the center of a customer's financial life. And those are two very different businesses. Maybe the bulls are wrong. Maybe SoFi remains a successful digital bank and nothing more. But if the bulls are right, investors looking back two years from now won't be talking about SOFIE, the 4.4% yield, or next quarter's earnings. They'll be talking about how the market spent years valuing a rapidly expanding financial technology platform as if it were just another bank. And by the time Wall Street realizes the difference, the stock may no longer be priced like one.

If SoFi eventually reaches $100 billion in deposits, it's not hard to imagine earnings power of $3 to $5 per share annually, especially if Anthony Noto continues to monetize those deposits across lending, investing, payments, subscriptions, and digital assets.
